newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil prices end off on views of ample supply.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil prices end off on views of ample supply.

text.p: NYMEX oil prices settled sharply lower Wednesday after an oil industry trade group reported rising inventories and said gasoline supplies were sufficient enough to meet even the most aggressive demand estimates.
"Prices had been rising on positive headlines this week, but things just deteriorated after the APIs came out. We are going to be testing lower levels again," said a New York crude trader.
May gasoline ended 1.52 cents lower at 60.38 cents a gallon.
May crude fell 48 cents to $19.35 a barrel while May heating oil finished 1.37 cents lower at 53.48 cents a gallon.

On Wednesday, The American Petroleum Institute (API) said in its annual outlook for the summer peak driving season that U.S. gasoline supplies should be sufficient to accomodate a 2.5 percent growth rate in demand, which is the upper range of estimates.

The outlook followed API's weekly oil inventory data it released Tuesday evening which said gasoline stocks swelled 3.63 million barrels compared with a one to two million barrel decline expected by traders.
The API oil inventory data reflects the week ended April 11.

Gasoline implied demand fell to a seasonally weak 7.3 million barrels per day (bpd) compared with 8.1 million bpd the week before. Gasoline demand is supposed to increase in the spring and summer and provide a bullish underpinning to the market, dealers said.
The market was undermined further by bearish builds in crude stocks and distillate stocks, which include heating oil and diesel.
Crude stocks rose 2.97 million barrels compared with a one million barrel build anticipated by traders. This is the sixth consecutive weekly crude stock build.
Crude stocks are now 11.3 million barrels higher than a year ago in the U.S. Gulf where refinery demand is concentrated.
Despite unseasonably cold weather in the key heating oil market of the U.S. Northeast, distillate stocks grew 2.59 million barrels when traders expected a decline of 1.5 million barrels.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
